about.title: Engineering from first principles to hardware.
paragraphs: I am pursuing a B.S. in Mechanical Engineering at Harvard College with a minor in Mathematical Sciences. My coursework includes computer-aided machine design, mechanical systems, solid and computational mechanics, and robotics.

My experience is strongly fabrication-driven: manual and CNC machining, welding, 3D printing, laser and waterjet cutting, soldering, CAD/CAE, embedded controls, fixture design, testing, and iterative build work.
Outside coursework, I lead and contribute to rocketry and robotics programs, work in research environments, and build personal projects ranging from CNC equipment to vehicle restoration.

fud.title: Forward Unto Dawn — Regeneratively Cooled Liquid Bipropellant Engine
fud.summary: Internally developed regeneratively cooled liquid-engine program where my current ownership is Chief Engineer oversight, PM, design-review leadership, and test/safety process development rather than detailed propulsion design.
fud.desc: Forward Unto Dawn is HUAC-R’s internally developed regeneratively cooled liquid-engine program. Through the current phase, my role has been primarily Chief Engineer and project management: reviewing and signing off on technical material, organizing design reviews, challenging assumptions and risks, and developing the test/safety process. Detailed CEA/RPA, cooling, injector, structural, and chamber-CAD work belongs to the subsystem designers and is presented only as project context.
fud.contrib: Reviewed/approved project scope and technical material, hosted and coordinated design reviews, provided technical feedback across disciplines, and co-developed the formal cold-flow/static-fire SOP and staged test campaign. I expect to take a more direct hardware role as full-team operations resume.
fud.result: In progress — analytical and early hardware development underway; test campaign structured around cold-flow validation before short-duration and longer hot fires.

deepDive.label: Program Leadership & Design Reviews
deepDive.content:
Serve as Chief Engineer/PM rather than the detailed propulsion designer. I review proposals, analyses, CAD/manufacturing plans, unresolved risks, and test readiness; organize and host design reviews; and use reviews as decision gates before irreversible commitments such as ordering printed hardware.

My job is to ask for evidence, challenge assumptions, verify interfaces, and decide whether risks have been sufficiently addressed—not to claim authorship of the underlying CEA, regen, injector, structural, or CAD work.

deepDive.label: Test & Safety Process Development
deepDive.content:
Co-developed the formal cold-flow/static-fire SOP, translating the engine program into a staged operational process covering assembly, mock-propellant cold flows, combined flow, controls/abort validation, igniter testing, short hot fire, longer hot fire, data collection, chemical handling, PPE, engineering controls, emergency response, and site logistics.

The test architecture deliberately retires risk before moving to more energetic stages and incorporates lessons learned from the Sphinx campaign.

deepDive.label: Technical Oversight & Readiness
deepDive.content:
Review scope includes performance/thermal tradeoffs, additive-manufacturing constraints, injector tolerances, feed-system architecture, instrumentation, material compatibility, hardware nonconformances, and test plans. I also require unresolved risks to remain visible rather than being buried at review.

Current ownership boundary is explicit: program leadership, technical review, safety/test documentation, and engineering approval are mine; detailed propulsion calculations and current engine geometry are team context unless I directly contribute to them later.

deepDive.label: Next Phase
deepDive.content: As full-team meetings and build work resume, I plan to become more directly involved in hardware integration, cold-flow execution, test-stand operations, and static-fire preparation while continuing Chief Engineer responsibilities.

rocketlink.title: RocketLink — Long-Range Rocket Telemetry System
rocketlink.summary: LoRa/GPS/IMU telemetry program developed from breadboard prototype through flight-adjacent packaged hardware, with my ownership spanning all mechanical enclosures plus Chief Engineer and PM responsibilities.
rocketlink.desc: RocketLink transmits live rocket position and motion data to a ground station. I served as both Chief Engineer/project manager and the mechanical enclosure designer, so this project shows two levels of ownership: personally designing/manufacturing the packaging, while coordinating and reviewing the broader avionics, software, procurement, integration, and test program without claiming detailed electrical/software work as my own.
rocketlink.contrib: Personally designed and 3D printed all rocket-side and ground-station enclosures. I also planned meetings and design reviews, managed the BOM/Gantt/procurement, led testing, coordinated subsystem integration, and reviewed layouts and technical decisions before hardware purchases or design freezes.
rocketlink.result: Progressed from breadboard proof-of-concept to V1 packaged protoboard hardware and a more robust PCB-based V2 architecture driven by field and mechanical testing.

deepDive.label: Requirements, Architecture & Leadership
deepDive.content:
As Chief Engineer/PM, organized the project around acceptance criteria for sensor acquisition, LoRa transmission, live ground-station decoding, logging, sustained bench operation, outdoor link testing, and data plausibility. I maintained the schedule, BOM, procurement, meetings, design reviews, and integration gates.

I reviewed avionics/software decisions at the system level—range, update rate, mass, vibration, throughput, interfaces, packaging, and test evidence—while leaving detailed electrical and software implementation to the members who owned those subsystems.

deepDive.label: Mechanical Enclosure Design — My Technical Ownership
deepDive.content:
Designed all mechanical packaging for both the rocket avionics and ground station. The housings had to retain the ESP32/LoRa/GPS/IMU/battery hardware while providing antenna routing, connector and power access, cable management, transport protection, assembly access, and field usability.

V1 used printed PLA housings with retained protoboard electronics and a separate battery strategy. I designed the physical interfaces around the evolving electrical layout rather than treating the enclosure as a cosmetic shell.

deepDive.label: Testing, Failure Modes & V1 Feedback
deepDive.content:
Led bench, outdoor/range, integration, and mechanical robustness testing. One documented range test measured about -87 dBm RSSI at 170 m, while the mechanical validation philosophy explicitly pushed the package beyond stationary bench conditions.

Testing showed that individually wired/protoboard electronics and several external interfaces were too fragile for the intended environment. We identified weak solder joints, antenna/GPS retention, battery access, connector clearance, and lid robustness as redesign drivers.

deepDive.label: V2 Redesign & Operational Handoff
deepDive.content:
The team transitioned toward a PCB-based architecture to reduce fragile point-to-point wiring, while I redesigned the enclosure around the revised hardware: better battery accessibility, stronger GPS/antenna retention, increased external clearances, improved USB access, and a thicker/more robust slide-on lid interface.

The project also moved toward a documented operational system with setup, pre-launch checks, telemetry viewing, logging, troubleshooting, and repeatable handoff rather than a prototype only its original builders could operate.

sphinx.title: Mojave Sphinx — Liquid Bipropellant Rocket Build, Integration & Test Program
sphinx.summary: Open-source Half Cat Rocketry reference build used by HUAC-R to develop hands-on liquid-rocketry capability in machining, integration, static-fire operations, and instrumented cold-flow testing.
sphinx.desc: HUAC-R built Mojave Sphinx using Half Cat Rocketry’s published HCR-5100 design and documentation. The vehicle design, analysis, drawings, original BOM, and published procedures are Half Cat Rocketry’s work; I do not claim them as original design work. Our goal was to use the reference architecture as a practical training platform and then expand our own test capability through cold-flow characterization and data acquisition.
sphinx.contrib: My work combined hands-on hardware and project leadership: machining selected hardware, assembling propulsion and avionics subsystems, leading full-vehicle integration, developing/manufacturing/installing the static-test-stand concept, participating in the first static-fire attempt, and managing the Gantt chart, meetings, material flow, procurement, task coordination, and test readiness.
sphinx.result: Reference vehicle manufactured and integrated; first static-fire attempt exposed fluid-system/sealing issues. Instrumented cold-flow characterization and a second static-fire campaign are in development.

deepDive.label: Build, Machining & Integration
deepDive.content:
Executed the published Half Cat architecture rather than redesigning the vehicle. I drilled the tank body, manufactured a quick-disconnect component, assembled servo-actuated propellant valves, bulkheads/interface hardware, the thrust chamber and avionics sled, supported piston installation, and helped bring the individual subsystems into the full vehicle.

The most useful learning came from real integration: seals, fittings, alignment, access, interfaces, and manufacturing dependencies that are much less obvious from drawings alone.

deepDive.label: Test Infrastructure & Static Fire
deepDive.content:
Developed the concept for HUAC-R’s dedicated static-fire restraint infrastructure and personally manufactured, assembled, and helped install the stand at the test site. I then integrated the vehicle with the stand/GSE and participated directly in static-fire preparation and operations.

The first attempt was unsuccessful because of fluid-system/sealing problems. That failure became a test-program input rather than an endpoint: we identified the need for stronger pre-fire characterization and verification before the next attempt.

deepDive.label: Cold-Flow Characterization
deepDive.content:
HUAC-R is now extending beyond the reference build with a dedicated cold-flow campaign. The current procedure uses non-combusting fluids to exercise the integrated feed system, hold pressure, identify leaks, cycle seals/valves, and observe flow through the injector/nozzle before ignition.

Before cold flow, we plan to design and integrate a data-acquisition system so the campaign produces quantitative characterization data rather than only qualitative observations. The exact instrumentation is still being selected, so I am intentionally not claiming measurements that have not yet been implemented.

deepDive.label: Project Leadership & Ownership
deepDive.content:
Managed the project Gantt chart, meeting/build organization, material and procurement flow, task coordination, build status, and test logistics while remaining directly involved in the hardware.

Ownership boundary: Half Cat owns the reference vehicle design/documentation. My technical ownership is in manufacturing, assembly/integration, test-stand implementation, testing, troubleshooting, and HUAC-R’s developing characterization process.

urc.title: University Rover Challenge — Manufacturing, DFM & Team Leadership
urc.summary: Primary machinist and team-level PM for a URC rover: completed or assisted with ~90% of robotic-arm mill/lathe parts while coordinating training, schedule, documentation, and cross-team execution.
urc.desc: The URC rover combined a lightweight chassis, four-wheel rocker suspension, six-DOF arm, science payload, electronics, and software. I did not personally design the entire rover or arm. My primary technical contribution was manufacturing and DFM; my broader contribution was team-level project management, manufacturing coordination, documentation, training, and cross-subsystem oversight.
urc.contrib: Completed or directly assisted with approximately 90% of robotic-arm components requiring mill/lathe work; provided DFM feedback and CAM solutions; supported assembly/troubleshooting; co-wrote the mechanical SAR; coordinated shop training; created/managed the full-team Gantt; documented lead meetings; delegated/tracked tasks; and led SolidWorks drawing workshops.
urc.result: Manufactured and integrated competition rover hardware; team arm validation demonstrated reliable loading up to ~7.5 kg under appropriate current/acceleration constraints.

deepDive.label: Precision Manufacturing & DFM
deepDive.content:
Manufactured the large majority of mill/lathe hardware for the six-DOF arm, including power-transmission and interface components. Work required manual/CNC turning and milling, workholding, machining sequence planning, bearing/shaft/gearbox interfaces, fits, and translation of team drawings into physical hardware.

I also reviewed designs for manufacturability. A representative coupler contained an internal hex that would effectively have required EDM; I proposed dog-ear corner reliefs so the corners could be drilled and the remaining profile CNC machined, then developed the machining approach in SolidWorks CAM.

deepDive.label: Assembly, Integration & Troubleshooting
deepDive.content:
Supported assembly of the machined arm hardware and cross-subsystem integration with motor controllers, encoders, Jetson/Teensy hardware, and power distribution. Testing progressed from individual joints to the assembled arm, load testing, and positioning work.

I also helped resolve mechanical issues discovered in use, including excessive differential-bar play and a repeatedly loosening rocker/differential set-screw connection.

deepDive.label: Project Management & Team Operations
deepDive.content:
Created and managed the full-team Gantt chart across mechanical, electrical, software, science, machining, integration, and testing. Took lead-meeting notes, tracked action items and dependencies, delegated work, coordinated testing windows, and maintained systems-level awareness beyond the parts I personally machined.

Worked with the Mechanical Lead to write the mechanical SAR, documenting team design rationale and validation without claiming authorship of mechanisms I did not design.

deepDive.label: Training & Team Capacity
deepDive.content:
Coordinated machine-shop training and prerequisite safety paperwork for new members, helped establish multiple shop-training pathways, and led workshops on creating manufacturing drawings from SolidWorks parts.

I also helped structure onboarding projects, created the club-fair poster, and supported recruitment/onboarding so the team could build long-term CAD and manufacturing capability rather than depend on a few experienced members.

ability.title: Servo-Driven Visual Perturbation Headset
ability.summary: Low-cost experimental headset using servo-driven mirrors to induce controlled balance perturbations.
ability.desc: Redesign of a visual-perturbation headset used in balance research. The original acrylic-and-tape assembly was replaced with a lighter, mechanically constrained, serviceable 3D-printed system.
ability.contrib: Redesigned the headset architecture in CAD, replaced taped acrylic construction with 3D-printed PLA and rigid mechanical joints, redesigned the servo-driven rotational axis and mirror retention, added PCB mounting, and iterated the assembly from captive-nut joints to heat-set inserts.

deepDive.label: Problem & Architecture
deepDive.content: Redesigned an inherited balance-perturbation headset that had been built from laser-cut acrylic and duct tape. The goal was a lighter, more rigid, repeatable, and serviceable research assembly while preserving the servo-driven mirror behavior required by the experiment.

deepDive.label: Mechanical Redesign
deepDive.content: Replaced taped acrylic construction with 3D-printed PLA, interlocking geometry, and mechanical fasteners. Iterated joints from captive nuts to heat-set inserts, added weight-relief features, and used a multibody/master-CAD strategy to preserve relationships as the design changed.

deepDive.label: Servo, Mirrors & Electronics Integration
deepDive.content: Redesigned the servo rotational interface, retained the moving mirror with a slot/set-screw strategy, clamped the second mirror between planar surfaces, and added dedicated PCB mounting rather than Velcro. These changes improved stability while keeping the system accessible for research use.

deepDive.label: Outcome & Lessons
deepDive.content: The rigid printed architecture was substantially more stable and lighter than the original 1/8-inch acrylic system. The project reinforced the value of serviceable joints, controlled constraints, and master-model CAD for iterative research hardware.

mahi.title: 3D-Printed TPU Force-Sensing Hardware for Biomedical Research
mahi.summary: Iterative wearable-sensor research spanning equation-driven CAD, conductive/flexible TPU process development, embedded electronics, 125-trial Instron calibration, serviceability redesign, and lab process documentation.
mahi.desc: At Rice University’s MAHI Lab, I developed customizable TPU housings for FSR-based biomedical sensing: a center-of-pressure insole and a scoliosis-brace force sensor. The work became a full design-build-test research loop involving many CAD generations, material/process characterization, embedded wiring, calibration hardware/software, failure analysis, and redesign for serviceability.
mahi.contrib: Developed equation-driven insole CAD, iterated 9+ insole and 15+ brace-sensor revisions, tested wire-retention and conductive-TPU geometries, developed multi-material print workflows, ran ~125 FSR/Instron trials, analyzed inconsistent electrical interfaces, created two pop-on-cover revisions, and documented repeatable TPU/multimaterial workflows for future lab users.
mahi.result: Validated brace-sensor embedded FSR behavior against controls; identified repeatability limitations in the fully encapsulated insole and developed a serviceable architecture; presented the work in a research poster.

deepDive.label: Design Evolution & Parametric CAD
deepDive.content:
Redesigned an inherited long-tail-FSR insole toward shorter-tail sensors and smaller/customizable sizing. Built equation-driven SolidWorks geometry so insole dimensions, sensor locations, and wire routing could scale together. The insole progressed through 9+ major revisions plus integrated assemblies and two serviceable-cover versions; the scoliosis-brace sensor progressed through at least V15.

The brace work similarly focused on reducing size, improving integration, and developing practical attachment strategies for brace- or skin-side use.

deepDive.label: Additive Manufacturing & Embedded Electronics
deepDive.content:
Developed internal wire channels, wire-retention test geometries, conductive-TPU specimens, and paused-print workflows for embedding FSRs/wires inside flexible TPU. Compared conductive materials and used small test coupons to learn faster before committing to full insole prints.

I also documented Bambu H2D TPU loading/settings and a SolidWorks multibody → Save Bodies → aligned STL workflow for repeatable multi-material printing, turning trial-and-error into a lab process other researchers could reproduce.

deepDive.label: Calibration & Experimental Validation
deepDive.content:
Built/used voltage-divider and microcontroller acquisition setups and connected the FSR system to an Instron so known compressive loads could be compared against sensor voltage. Evaluated multiple divider resistances and completed approximately 125 trials, with Python/serial logging and post-processing.

Embedded brace sensors produced output comparable to controls, while some insole sensors did not—showing that the sensor concept could work but the integrated electrical interfaces were not yet sufficiently repeatable.

deepDive.label: Failure Analysis, Serviceability & Research Outcome
deepDive.content:
The fully encapsulated insole was elegant but difficult to debug or repair when conductive-TPU/electrical interfaces were inconsistent. I redesigned the architecture around a removable pop-on cover so electronics could be installed and serviced after the main body was printed.

The project culminated in a research poster plus CAD/STL libraries, material specimens, calibration circuitry/code/data, and process documentation. A major lesson was that “fully integrated” is not automatically better when research hardware must remain serviceable and diagnosable.

yellow.title: Yellow Jacket Competition Robot
yellow.summary: Competition robot that collected tennis balls, placed them on a Velcro wall, and climbed 15° and 30° inclines.
yellow.desc: A semester-long Turf Wars machine-design competition robot built to place tennis balls onto a wall with three scoring heights. Our team prioritized scoring quantity, ultimately developing an “egg-carton flipper” capable of placing four balls at once.
yellow.contrib: Developed 100% of the final robot CAD, helped prototype the mechanism in cardboard, and contributed substantially to manufacturing and assembly. The project introduced me to machining through operations including milling wheel molds, turning shafts, and fabricating angle-bracket components.

deepDive.label: Requirements, Concepts & Prototyping
deepDive.content:
Designed for a 12×12×12 in Turf Wars envelope: collect tennis balls, climb 15°/30° ramps, and score on a Velcro wall. We compared Archimedes-screw, conveyor, and multi-ball flipper concepts, selecting the flipper for capacity, packaging, low center of gravity, manufacturability, and reduced actuator count. A cardboard prototype validated the basic scoring mechanism before full CAD.

The intake evolved from a Velcro-covered duct-tape-roll test into a servo-driven roller with reduced Velcro and a mechanical stripping edge so balls released into the hopper instead of remaining attached.

deepDive.label: CAD, Analysis & Design Ownership
deepDive.content:
Personally completed 100% of the final robot CAD, including parts and assembly. The drivetrain used four-wheel belt drive, selected motors, a 3:1 ratio, and cast silicone wheels for traction. We also performed torque, friction, distributed-load, bending, and stress/strain calculations to check drivetrain and structure.

A major design tradeoff was removing a vertical extension mechanism: it sacrificed access to the highest scoring zone but made the final system simpler, stronger, and more reliable.

deepDive.label: Manufacturing & Integration
deepDive.content:
Manufacturing included laser-cut acrylic, CNC-milled wheel molds, silicone casting, 3D-printed pulleys/intake parts, lathe-turned shafts, bandsaw-cut brackets, drilled/tapped features, and CNC-milled Delrin supports.

Tight drivetrain tolerances and CAD errors created assembly issues that could not be solved by a belt tensioner alone, forcing physical modification and becoming an early lesson in tolerance management and DFM.

deepDive.label: Testing, Competition & Outcome
deepDive.content:
Yellow Jacket climbed both ramps, reliably collected balls, and placed up to four balls at once. A loaded flipper could score six points in one action; the robot scored up to 12 points, required only one competition “life,” and finished 2nd overall.

Final specs included 3.75 kg mass, 8 in height, 11.25 in width, 12 in length, 1.125 in undercarriage clearance, 5.86 in turning radius, 3:1 drivetrain ratio, and 4:1 scoring-mechanism ratio.

nerf.title: Red Light–Green Light Nerf Turret
nerf.summary: Squid Game-inspired Red Light–Green Light Nerf turret using five PIR sensors, Arduino logic, servos, and a rotating mechanical platform.
nerf.desc: A Red Light–Green Light-inspired mechatronics system that used five PIR sensors to detect motion during the green-light state and command a rotating Nerf turret to aim and fire. The project combined Arduino control logic, sensor segmentation, servo actuation, laser-cut structures, acrylic, and iterative mechanical troubleshooting.
nerf.contrib: Worked across both the electrical and mechanical systems: developed and expanded the PIR sensing logic, prototyped sensor view windows and aiming geometry, contributed to the laser-cut enclosure and rotating turret architecture, and helped troubleshoot actuator torque and late-stage mechanical failures during the SEAS Design Fair.
nerf.result: Functional course-final turret demonstrated at the SEAS Design Fair after rapid on-site mechanical repairs and actuator redesigns.

deepDive.label: System Architecture & PIR Prototyping
deepDive.content:
Built a Squid Game-inspired Red Light–Green Light turret using five PIR sensors, Arduino state logic, a rotating Nerf platform, and a trigger servo. We chose PIR after considering pressure plates, ranging, wearables, and vision because it provided simple motion detection and let us discretize the field into five target zones.

I focused heavily on code/prototyping: started with one PIR, expanded to five, implemented game-state logic, debouncing, first-detection lockout, randomized timing, and mapped sensor zones to turret angles.

deepDive.label: Mechanical Design & Integration
deepDive.content:
Prototyped PIR field-of-view separation in foam board before moving to rigid divider panels and printed mounts. The Nerf gun sat on a laser-cut acrylic disk supported by a ball-bearing track; physical stoplights used wooden structures and acrylic diffusers.

Integration exposed practical issues including breadboard accessibility, LED power demand, bearing-track rigidity, and the fact that flexible prototype geometry did not translate directly into rigid construction.

deepDive.label: Actuation, Torque & Iteration
deepDive.content: The turret servo lacked torque, so we reduced rotating mass with weight-relief cuts; a future design would add gearing. The trigger servo also lacked torque, so we added a gear train that increased available torque roughly threefold.

deepDive.label: Design-Fair Failure & Recovery
deepDive.content:
At the SEAS Design Fair, the geared trigger system over-traveled and broke the custom gun attachment. With no time for a new part, we drilled through the gun/attachment and zip-tied them together, keeping the system operational for the fair.

The failure was a direct lesson that solving an actuator-torque problem can create a new structural problem unless travel limits, stops, and downstream loads are also reconsidered.

bridge.title: Optimized I-Beam Bridge
bridge.summary: Wood bridge optimized for compression force-to-weight performance and tested in an Instron.
bridge.desc: A wood-and-acrylic bridge designed for a structural competition and compression-tested on an Instron. The bridge carried 16 kN—the highest absolute load in the competition—but placed second because ranking was based on force-to-weight ratio.
bridge.contrib: Designed and fabricated the bridge around an I-beam-inspired cross section, considered wood grain direction during manufacturing to avoid weak orientations, and incorporated acrylic into the upper structure for aesthetics. The acrylic added weight without meaningful structural benefit, which reduced the final force-to-weight score.

deepDive.label: Structural Design
deepDive.content: Used an I-beam-inspired cross section to increase bending and compressive performance while controlling mass.

deepDive.label: Material & Manufacturing Decisions
deepDive.content: Built primarily from wood with wood-glue assembly and intentionally oriented the wood grain to avoid creating weak directions. Acrylic was incorporated into the upper section for visual appeal.

deepDive.label: Instron Testing
deepDive.content: Compression-tested the completed bridge on an Instron. It sustained 16 kN, the highest absolute force in the competition.

deepDive.label: Outcome & Lessons
deepDive.content: The competition was scored by force-to-weight ratio, so the bridge placed second despite carrying the highest load. The acrylic aesthetic feature added mass without structural benefit, making it a clear lesson in aligning every design decision with the actual optimization metric.

egg.title: Variable-Damping Egg Drop System
egg.summary: Spring-damper protection system using shaped tracks to vary damping behavior through compression.
egg.desc: A dynamics competition project using springs, dampers, and laser-cut wood to protect an egg during impact. The damper traveled along mathematically designed tracks so its compression behavior varied through the impact stroke.
egg.contrib: Helped develop the mathematically driven variable-damping concept, fabricate the laser-cut structure, and test the system. The project also became a useful lesson in the difference between idealized models and real hardware behavior.

deepDive.label: Dynamics Model & Design Objective
deepDive.content: Designed a passive spring-damper suspension to minimize egg acceleration during impact under strict stroke/geometry constraints. Modeled the system as an equivalent 2-DOF spring-damper system and derived equations of motion using Lagrangian mechanics.

deepDive.label: Variable-Damping Track Optimization
deepDive.content: The core concept moved a damper endpoint along a nonlinear guide track so a constant physical damper produced a changing effective vertical damping response. A Python model represented the track with a fourth-order polynomial and used numerical optimization to seek near-constant deceleration over the available stopping distance.

deepDive.label: My Role, Prototyping & Manufacturing
deepDive.content: My role leaned toward project management plus analysis/prototyping rather than CAD ownership: I organized the timeline, worked on simulations, prototyping, assembly, and substantial final-report work. We built a cardboard prototype before the final laser-cut structure.

deepDive.label: Competition, Model vs. Hardware & Lessons
deepDive.content:
The physical mechanism did not reproduce the ideal model cleanly because friction, tolerances, binding, compliance, and alignment mattered. During competition, a structural corner fractured and unintentionally absorbed impact energy like a sacrificial element; the egg survived and the team placed 2nd.

That outcome made the project a useful lesson in both model fidelity and intentional energy absorption: an optimized mechanism must be physically realizable, and controlled sacrificial deformation can be a valid impact-management strategy.

abaqus.title: Parametric Kresling Origami Unit-Cell FEA Model
abaqus.summary: Python-driven Abaqus model varying side count, radius, and height to study compression response.
abaqus.desc: Developed and experimentally validated a nonlinear Abaqus model of a Kresling origami unit cell, then parameterized the geometry to study how side count, radius, and height affect compression response.
abaqus.contrib: Built the Python-driven geometry, shell/spring model architecture, boundary conditions, nonlinear stabilization strategy, experimental Instron validation, calibration, and geometry sweeps. The work included substantial debugging of failed CAD-import, hinge, convergence, and hysteresis approaches.
abaqus.result: Calibrated simulation matched effective physical stiffness closely (~906 N/mm simulation vs ~885 N/mm experiment) while also exposing limitations in reproducing unloading hysteresis.

deepDive.label: Model Architecture & Iteration
deepDive.content:
Started with SolidWorks/STEP geometry, but solid folded corners did not translate cleanly to the desired shell-and-hinge model. Rebuilt the unit cell directly in Abaqus using mathematically generated datum points, wire features, shell surfaces, and separate assembled facets so coincident edges could retain independent nodes.

Iterated through connector/merged-edge hinge approaches before settling on node-paired spring-dashpot connections with local coordinate systems.

deepDive.label: Python Parametric Geometry & Nonlinear FEA
deepDive.content:
Parameterized the Kresling geometry by polygon side count, radius, height, and twist angle. Python generated coordinates and model geometry so configurations could be swept systematically.

Used Static General with NLGEOM and tuned automatic stabilization after early simulations aborted or snapped unrealistically. Boundary conditions fixed the bottom and displacement-controlled the top through a reference point while allowing rotation.

deepDive.label: Physical Prototype, Instron & Calibration
deepDive.content:
3D printed physical unit cells, transitioning from brittle small PLA prototypes to a larger ABS model. Compressed the ABS cell 10 mm on an Instron and cycled it 10 times to investigate force-displacement response and hysteresis.

Used experimental data to calibrate torsional spring stiffness. Effective stiffness was approximately 885 N/mm physically versus 906 N/mm in simulation.

deepDive.label: Parameter Sweeps, Limits & Lessons
deepDive.content:
Swept polygon side count from 5–10 and radius from 2–8 cm at fixed height to study geometry-dependent stiffness. The model captured effective loading stiffness but not physical unloading hysteresis; adding simple ABS plasticity produced unrealistic permanent deformation.

The project became as much about model architecture and debugging as final plots: isolate mechanisms, validate simple submodels, and distinguish “matches one property” from “reproduces the full physics.”

controls.title: Friction & Backlash Identification and Compensation Platform
controls.summary: Experimental controls platform that varied friction and backlash in a brushless-motor transmission, then used collected data to develop a PID controller with compensation.
controls.desc: Designed and experimentally validated a single-joint robotic test platform that deliberately varied friction and backlash, identified those nonlinearities from data, and incorporated them into a compensated controller.
controls.contrib: Helped design/build the adjustable mechanical apparatus and instrumentation, developed/used MATLAB models, ran a 20-condition experiment, processed motor/encoder/current data, identified Coulomb friction and backlash, and contributed to the compensated controller and validation.
controls.result: Primary validation condition reduced tracking-error range by ~50% versus baseline PID, while also revealing increased current demand and hardware safety limits at extreme conditions.

deepDive.label: Modeling & Experimental Apparatus
deepDive.content:
Started with a 1-DOF rotational MATLAB model and explored friction/backlash representations before building a modular physical platform with a DC gearmotor, motor-side incremental encoder, load-side SSI absolute encoder, interchangeable backlash components, and adjustable friction clamp.

Baseline PID was tuned to Kp=1.5, Ki=0.5, Kd=0.05 before introducing controlled nonlinearities.

deepDive.label: Controlled Nonlinearities & Data Collection
deepDive.content: Created four friction conditions using clamp adjustment and multiple backlash couplers spanning nominal 0.1–0.5 mm geometry changes. Conducted 20 experimental trials and logged reference position, both encoder signals, PWM, direction, state, and motor current—roughly 995 samples per trial.

deepDive.label: System Identification & Controller Development
deepDive.content:
Selected a Coulomb friction model after comparing alternatives and corrected an early sign/direction implementation error. Replaced an assumed backlash dead-zone width with event-based identification: backlash was detected when the motor encoder moved while the load encoder remained nearly stationary.

Used identified friction as feedforward compensation and measured backlash to modify the desired motor-side motion.

deepDive.label: Validation, Tradeoffs & Lessons
deepDive.content:
In the primary low-friction/low-backlash validation case, tracking-error range dropped from roughly 60 to 30 encoder ticks. Compensation continued to improve tracking as nonlinearities increased, but required more reversals/torque and caused current surges.

At the most extreme conditions, current safety limits prevented full evaluation—an important reminder that better control performance can create electrical/thermal costs. Future work would quantify friction more directly and smooth/current-limit compensation.

plasma.desc: An in-progress custom 3-axis CNC plasma cutter designed around a standard removable hand-held plasma torch. deepDive.label: System Concept
deepDive.content: The machine uses a standard hand-held plasma torch mounted to the CNC end effector so the torch can be removed and used independently. The goal is to gain CNC capability without permanently modifying or dedicating the existing plasma cutter.

deepDive.label: Mechanical Architecture
deepDive.content: All three axes use belt-driven motion with V-slot wheels riding on aluminum extrusion and NEMA stepper motors providing actuation. Custom structural and interface parts are designed for 3D-printed PLA, while the aluminum extrusion is cut to length for the frame.

deepDive.label: Z-Axis & Torch Height
deepDive.content: The end effector includes a motor-driven lead-screw linear actuator for focus/height adjustment. The planned automatic-focus workflow uses material thickness as an input and adds a probing sensor on the Z axis to establish the work surface.

deepDive.label: Controls & GRBL
deepDive.content: Machine motion is programmed around Arduino and the GRBL controller. The interface is planned to accept job/material information and coordinate axis motion through the standard GRBL workflow.

deepDive.label: Plasma-Cutter Integration
deepDive.content: Because the plasma cutter cannot be electrically modified, the software will recommend torch settings based on the selected material and thickness, but the user will set those parameters manually. The machine can indicate when it is ready to cut, while plasma ignition remains a separate manual action.

deepDive.label: User Interface
deepDive.content: The planned user interface will be hosted from a GitHub repository and will provide a cleaner front end for machine setup, material inputs, and the CNC workflow.

deepDive.content: Mechanical design and manufacturing are underway. The current target is to complete the machine by December 2026, followed by calibration, probing integration, and cutting validation.

stocksmart.desc: Semester-long client-driven design project for the Wyss Institute. A 16-person multidisciplinary team first had to identify which institutional problem was worth solving, then develop an integrated NFC-based stockroom management concept.
stocksmart.contrib: My role was primarily PM/systems-level design rather than CAD/software implementation: I did substantial problem-statement definition, created the decision matrix, documented concept/problem elimination, helped organize the broad system architecture and cross-team work, discussed design ideas with the CAD team, and wrote a substantial portion of the 110-page final report.
stocksmart.result: Delivered an integrated prototype concept spanning NFC/HUID mobile checkout, administrative inventory software, and dedicated phone hardware to support item-level usage billing and inventory visibility.

deepDive.label: Client Research & Problem Definition
deepDive.content:
The team spent ~5 weeks researching/interviewing across Wyss groups and generated 13 candidate problem statements spanning transportation, operations, communication, and research-specific needs. I helped synthesize the research and personally documented why problems were merged, reframed, retained, or eliminated.

The final stockroom problem emerged from a real billing/inventory pain point: per-visit charging could create inequity while item-level inventory remained largely manual.

deepDive.label: Trade Study & Solution Selection
deepDive.content:
After ideation, we narrowed to pressure-plate/smart-shelf, software-only, and NFC-phone concepts. I created the weighted decision matrix using criteria including cost, backend ease, user experience, time efficiency, robustness to error, adaptability, adoptability, loss prevention, and scope.

The NFC-phone concept ranked highest because it balanced accountability, user experience, adaptability, and implementation feasibility.

deepDive.label: Systems Architecture & Cross-Team Coordination
deepDive.content:
The final system combined a mobile app, backend/admin website, NFC/HUID workflow, and a wall-mounted charging station. I was not on the dedicated CAD/software teams; my contribution was maintaining the broad architecture and interfaces, discussing design ideas, and helping the frontend, backend, and hardware workstreams stay aligned.

Client feedback drove important workflow changes, including support for researchers belonging to multiple labs/grants.

deepDive.label: Documentation, PM & Outcome
deepDive.content:
Wrote a substantial portion of the 110-page final report and helped structure it around the full engineering process: research → problem synthesis → elimination → definition → ideation → decision matrix → prototyping → final design → implementation.

This project is strongest evidence of problem definition, structured decision-making, systems thinking, technical writing, and PM—not of personal CAD ownership.

square-pendulum.title: 2D Coupled Pendula — Normal Modes of a Square System
square-pendulum.summary: Combined analytical, MATLAB, and physical modeling study of the normal modes of a square pendulum system.
square-pendulum.desc: Extended the familiar 1D coupled-pendulum problem into a four-pendulum square system, combining a custom mechanical apparatus, accelerometer instrumentation, Arduino acquisition, Python logging, MATLAB frequency/phase analysis, and simulation.
square-pendulum.contrib: Designed and assembled the physical setup, built the electronics, wrote Arduino acquisition code, developed the Python serial logger and MATLAB FFT/phase analysis pipeline, and compared candidate normal modes against simulation and experiment.
square-pendulum.result: Classified 11 candidate motions and found that in 2D, initial position alone is not enough to define a normal mode—the initial velocity state can also be essential.

deepDive.label: Apparatus & Instrumentation
deepDive.content:
Built a square array of four spring-coupled pendula with a visual XY grid and instrumented two pendula with dual-axis ADXL335 accelerometers. Dummy wiring on the remaining pendula reduced sensor-wiring asymmetry.

Arduino acquisition sampled internally at high rate with filtering/gravity subtraction; a Python logger handled serial connection, trial IDs, timestamps, and CSV output.

deepDive.label: Experimental Design
deepDive.content: Tested 11 initial displacement/motion schemes—including symmetric, antisymmetric, breathing, radial, trapezoidal, rectangular, circular, and assisted rotating motions—with ~25 s of data per trial and a stationary baseline period.

deepDive.label: Signal Processing & Simulation
deepDive.content: MATLAB detrended and plotted accelerometer histories, used FFT/power spectra to identify dominant frequencies, and used cross-power spectral density to examine phase relationships. A computational model predicted ideal pendulum trajectories for comparison.

deepDive.label: Results & Physical Insight
deepDive.content:
Symmetric, antisymmetric, breathing, rectangle, and assisted-parallel-rotating configurations were classified as normal under appropriate initial conditions. The apparently symmetric circular case was not normal; energy transferred between modes and trajectories became square-like.

The assisted rotating case showed that a correct initial velocity can be required in 2D, making the state definition richer than simply specifying initial displacement.

heat-transfer.title: IR & Hyperspectral Detection of Plant Drought Stress
heat-transfer.summary: Two-week experiment using six fern plants, controlled watering levels, and daily IR imaging to investigate whether thermal imagery can reveal drought stress before plant death.
heat-transfer.desc: Investigated whether thermal IR and hyperspectral measurements could reveal drought stress, pivoting from an uncontrolled outdoor tree study to a controlled six-fern watering experiment and complementary remote-sensing analysis.
heat-transfer.contrib: Helped redefine the research question after weak field results, designed/ran the controlled fern study, collected and analyzed repeated IR measurements, expanded analysis beyond a single centerpoint, and connected the thermal results to NDVI/NDWI hyperspectral drought indicators.
heat-transfer.result: Controlled data supported warmer plant temperatures under water stress and showed the coolest/stablest response at moderate watering; hyperspectral analysis independently connected low NDWI to lower vegetation water content.

deepDive.label: Research Question & Experimental Pivot
deepDive.content: The original plan compared outdoor trees, but environmental variability and difficulty identifying comparable stressed vegetation produced weak, non-significant differences. Rather than force a conclusion, we redesigned the project around a controlled independent variable: water availability.

deepDive.label: Controlled Fern Experiment
deepDive.content:
Used six identical ferns with watering schedules from none to twice daily and collected repeated IR images before watering across ~15 measurement sessions. One fan-on datapoint visibly demonstrated the effect of convective conditions and why environmental control mattered.

Analysis expanded from the camera centerpoint to a larger region around the fern to examine spatial temperature variation.

deepDive.label: IR Results
deepDive.content: The no-water fern was consistently among the hottest, while the twice-weekly condition was coolest and most stable. Daily/twice-daily watering did not provide additional cooling and showed greater variability, suggesting the response was nonlinear rather than simply “more water = colder.”

deepDive.label: Hyperspectral Analysis & Takeaways
deepDive.content:
Analyzed NASA airborne hyperspectral data using NDVI to identify vegetation and NDWI to evaluate water content. Lower NDWI corresponded to greater SWIR response and drier vegetation.

The two methods provide complementary physics: reduced water limits transpiration/evaporative cooling and raises thermal temperature, while lower tissue water changes SWIR absorption. The strongest project lesson was experimental judgment—recognizing when the first design could not answer the question and rebuilding the study around controlled variables.

senior-thesis.title: Reconfigurable Loudspeaker Enclosure — Senior Capstone
senior-thesis.summary: In-progress senior capstone exploring a loudspeaker enclosure that collapses for transport and expands into repeatable acoustically useful configurations.
senior-thesis.desc: Starting Fall 2026, my capstone investigates whether the enclosure itself can become reconfigurable, addressing the tradeoff between portable speaker size and the internal volume needed for predictable acoustic performance. The project is currently in problem-definition and early design; no prototype/test results are claimed yet.
senior-thesis.contrib: Mechanical design/manufacturing lead. Planned ownership includes enclosure CAD, deployment/locking mechanisms, focused mechanism prototypes, manufacturing, and mechanical validation, coordinated with my partner’s speaker/electrical/sensing work.
senior-thesis.result: In progress — requirements, architecture space, validation strategy, and project roadmap established; concept development and focused prototyping next.

deepDive.label: Problem, Requirements & System Architecture
deepDive.content:
Treating the speaker as a coupled mechanical-electrical-acoustic system. Current targets include ≥50% reduction in stored bounding volume, <15 in maximum external dimension, <10 lb total system mass, collapsed plus at least two stable operating configurations, and repeatable internal volume within ±5%.

The first integrated prototype is planned as a sealed enclosure so volume changes have a comparatively direct acoustic interpretation.

deepDive.label: Mechanical Concept Space
deepDive.content: Evaluating telescoping rigid sections, origami/folding structures, compliant enclosures, and hybrid architectures that separate airtight sealing from structural stiffness. Key risks include leakage, rattling/binding, fold fatigue, wall compliance/resonance, wiring across moving interfaces, and locking repeatability.

deepDive.label: Validation Plan
deepDive.content: Planned validation compares the reconfigurable enclosure against an equivalent rigid reference: pressure-decay sealing, wall vibration, microphone frequency response, impedance, configuration detection, and repeated deployment. Current targets include ±3 dB acoustic agreement with the rigid reference, ±1 dB repeatability within a state, and 100 deployment cycles.

deepDive.label: Current Status & My Ownership
deepDive.content:
Current phase is proposal/define/early design. Next work is driver/volume selection, CAD concept generation, focused high-risk prototypes, concept selection, and integrated preliminary design.

My ownership is mechanical design, mechanism development, fabrication, and mechanical validation; my partner owns the primary speaker/electrical/sensing work.

engineering-music.title: Engineering Musical Instruments — Mechanical, Electronic & Electromechanical
engineering-music.summary: Three instrument builds exploring mechanical acoustics, wearable sensing/MIDI, and motor-driven frictional resonance.
engineering-music.desc: Across three course projects, I designed and built instruments that connected engineering decisions to musical behavior: a crank-driven pendulum glockenspiel, a force-sensitive wearable electronic piano, and a servo-driven glass “Harponica.”
engineering-music.contrib: Contributions included SolidWorks pulley/table CAD, belt and copper-bar fabrication, Arduino/MIDI sensor code and breadboarding, sensor calibration, servo wiring/control code, laser cutting, assembly, acoustic tuning, and iterative troubleshooting.
engineering-music.result: Three playable prototypes that exposed different interactions between tolerances, sensing, actuation, structural support, and acoustics.

deepDive.label: (Bi)Pendulum Glockenspiel
deepDive.content:
Built a crank-driven belt system carrying tuned copper bars past pendulum strikers. I designed printed pulleys, fabricated the belt from bicycle inner tube, drilled/threaded the copper bars, and operated the crank.

Iteration focused on acoustic freedom and tolerances: direct belt attachment damped the bars, so we moved to string suspension; a second pendulum added simultaneous notes; shaft/pulley fit errors required late-stage repair. The project showed that attachment stiffness and tolerance directly affect sound.

deepDive.label: Sept-Sensor Electric Piano
deepDive.content:
Developed a glove-based electronic instrument using seven FSRs as musical keys, with pressure thresholds controlling octave. I modified Arduino/MIDI code for analog force inputs, built the breadboard, characterized sensor thresholds, and supported wearable integration.

The original flex-sensor idea changed after discovering the available devices were linear potentiometers. Glove-mounted force transmission also changed calibration, and Arduino analog-input limitations reduced the final design from eight to seven keys.

deepDive.label: Glass Harponica
deepDive.content:
Built a semi-automated glass-harp/harmonica hybrid where seven water-tuned wine glasses rotated on continuous servos while the player held a damp finger stationary. I completed the tabletop CAD/laser cutting, organized servo wiring, and wrote the seven-servo Arduino control code.

The largest lesson was separating actuation from structural support: the servo shafts could rotate the glasses but were poor single-point supports for top-heavy water-filled loads. A future version would support the rotating plates on bearings while using the servos primarily for torque.

deepDive.label: Cross-Project Engineering Lessons
deepDive.content: Together the projects covered mechanical tolerancing and resonance, sensor calibration/HMI, and electromechanical actuation. They also repeatedly showed that the “musical” requirement is an engineering requirement: constraint stiffness, motor noise, water mass, sensor mounting, and manufacturing variation all changed the resulting sound/playability.

modular-test-stand.title: Modular Rocket Test Stand
modular-test-stand.summary: In-progress modular test-stand concept intended to support multiple future static-fire configurations.
modular-test-stand.desc: An in-progress test-infrastructure project intended to create a single modular stand that can be reconfigured for multiple future rocket static fires rather than building a new stand for each vehicle.
modular-test-stand.contrib: Developed early concepts for a vice-like adjustable rocket restraint, configurable mounting interfaces, and a translating support structure that can be repositioned and then mechanically locked in place.

deepDive.label: Current Concept
deepDive.content: The current concept uses a vice-like adjustable restraint for the rocket, multiple clearance holes and fastener locations for configurable mounting, and a mounting section that can translate linearly. Early concepts use spring-ball locating features similar to tent-pole mechanisms for adjustment, followed by positive bolting once the desired position is set.

machining-projects.title: Machining Projects — Brass Hammer
machining-projects.summary: Decorative brass hammer made on a manual lathe as a turning-practice project, using stepped geometry and hand finishing to create an ornate handle profile.
machining-projects.desc: A manual-lathe practice project focused on building turning skill through a small finished object. I made an ornate brass hammer with a handle inspired by candlesticks and decorative furniture legs, including a beaded profile produced through closely spaced stepped cuts and hand finishing.
machining-projects.contrib: Designed the visual profile, turned the brass components manually, created the decorative handle geometry through many small diameter steps, and progressively sanded the transitions until the stepped geometry became a smooth ornamental contour.

deepDive.label: Design Inspiration
deepDive.content: The handle profile was inspired by the ornamental forms found in candlesticks and turned table or chair legs, rather than a purely utilitarian hammer handle.

deepDive.label: Manual Turning
deepDive.content: The project was made on a manual lathe as deliberate practice in controlling diameters, shoulders, and surface finish in brass.

deepDive.label: Decorative Profile
deepDive.content: I created the beaded/ornamental section as a series of very small stepped diameter changes, gradually reducing the size of the steps to approximate the intended curved profile.

deepDive.label: Finishing
deepDive.content: The stepped surfaces were then sanded until the transitions blended into a continuous smooth contour, turning the discrete lathe cuts into the final decorative form.

mccannic-vehicle-mover.title: Shop Vehicle-Moving Grill Guard
mccannic-vehicle-mover.summary: MIG-welded angle-iron front attachment with tire sections used to push disabled vehicles short distances around an automotive repair shop.
mccannic-vehicle-mover.desc: A shop-fabrication project created to make it faster and easier to reposition disabled vehicles around an automotive repair facility without setting up a tow for every short movement. The device used a rigid angle-iron frame attached to the front of a shop truck, with tire sections providing a more compliant contact surface against the vehicle being moved.
mccannic-vehicle-mover.contrib: Cut, fit, and MIG-welded the angle-iron structure and helped assemble the tire-contact portions into the completed front-mounted vehicle-moving device.
mccannic-vehicle-mover.result: Completed shop tool used to move broken-down vehicles around the repair facility.

deepDive.label: Problem & Use Case
deepDive.content: The auto-repair shop needed a quick way to move disabled vehicles short distances around the property without repeatedly setting up conventional towing equipment.

deepDive.label: Concept
deepDive.content: The solution was a front-mounted steel guard on a shop truck that could contact and push another vehicle, with cut tire sections acting as compliant interfaces to reduce direct metal-to-vehicle contact.

deepDive.label: Fabrication
deepDive.content: The structure was built from angle iron that was cut, fitted, and MIG-welded into the front-mounted frame.

deepDive.label: Implementation
deepDive.content: Tire sections were attached to the completed guard, and the truck was then used as a practical shop vehicle mover for broken-down cars.
